title: Service Locator Pattern
oneLiner: Centralizes lookup of shared services through a registry that any code can query by name or type, instead of passing them around explicitly.

hero.name: The Directory
hero.catchphrase: Don't know where to find it? Ask me. I'll look it up.
hero.power: Centralizes shared service lookup through a single registry that any code can query on demand, wherever it happens to run.
hero.weakness: Hides a class's real dependencies inside its method bodies instead of its constructor — they become invisible until runtime, and harder to test than plain injection.
hero.origin: The Directory appeared inside a game engine where deeply nested gameplay code needed access to the AudioManager, but threading it through six layers of constructor parameters felt absurd.

story.problem: A deeply nested piece of gameplay code needs the AudioManager, six layers down from where the game loop starts. Threading it through every intermediate constructor as a parameter feels absurd for something used so rarely.
story.solution: The Directory introduces a `ServiceLocator` registry. Deep gameplay code just calls `ServiceLocator.get("audio")` when it actually needs sound, without every intermediate layer needing to know or pass it along.
story.result: Only the code that genuinely needs AudioManager touches it — via a lookup, not a six-layer parameter chain that clutters every constructor in between.

before: A rarely-used dependency is threaded through many constructor layers
Every intermediate layer must know about a dependency it never uses
Adding a new deep dependency means touching every layer in between
after: Deep code looks up rarely-used dependencies on demand
Intermediate layers stay unaware of dependencies they don't use
Adding a new deep dependency touches only the code that needs it

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Six constructors in a row each accept an AudioManager parameter just to pass it further down, unused.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I'm threading AudioManager through six constructors that never even use it, just so the seventh layer can play one sound effect.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Directory appears holding a single lookup book, ready to hand out any service by name, on demand.
panels.speaker: The Directory
panels.dialogue: Stop threading it through six layers that don't need it. When you actually need AudioManager, just ask ME.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: ServiceLocator.get('audio') looks up and returns the registered AudioManager instance, wherever it's called.
panels.speaker: The Directory
panels.dialogue: Only the deep code that genuinely needs audio calls me. The five layers between game-loop and gameplay-code stay untouched.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Six constructor signatures shrink back down. Only the actual sound-playing code touches AudioManager at all.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Six constructors are clean again. Only the one function that actually plays a sound touches AudioManager now.

useWhen: A dependency is genuinely rarely used, deep in a call chain, and threading it through every intermediate layer via constructor injection is impractical.
You're working in a framework or engine (like many game engines) where global registries are an established convention.
You accept the trade-off of hidden dependencies in exchange for avoiding excessive parameter threading.
avoidWhen: Dependency Injection (passing dependencies explicitly through constructors) is practical — DI keeps dependencies visible and is generally easier to test.
You want a class's dependencies to be discoverable just by reading its constructor signature.
You need strong compile-time guarantees that a required service is actually available — Service Locator's lookups typically fail at runtime instead.
commonMistakes: Reaching for Service Locator as a default instead of Dependency Injection, hiding dependencies that should be visible and explicit.
Letting the locator's registry grow into a dumping ground for every shared object in the app, becoming an untracked global state store.
Not handling missing registrations gracefully, letting `get()` fail with a confusing runtime error far from where the actual bug is.
Making testing harder than it needs to be — since dependencies are hidden inside method bodies, mocking them requires manipulating the global locator instead of a simple constructor argument.
explanation.realWorldExample: Game engines' global manager registries (Unity's `FindObjectOfType`, older engine `ServiceLocator` classes), and some legacy Java EE JNDI lookups, are real-world Service Locator implementations — though modern guidance generally favors Dependency Injection where practical.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Why wouldn't I just always use you instead of threading dependencies through constructors?

conversation.speaker: The Directory
conversation.message: Because I hide what a class actually depends on. Read Enemy's constructor and you'd never know it needs AudioManager — that only shows up buried inside onDeath(). DI keeps dependencies visible; I trade that visibility for convenience.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So when do you actually win?

conversation.speaker: The Directory
conversation.message: When threading a genuinely rare dependency through many layers that never use it would be worse than the hidden-dependency trade-off. Use me sparingly, and prefer DI whenever it's practical.

codeBattle.scenario: Your game's deeply nested combat-resolution code occasionally needs to play a sound effect, but it's called from twelve different places across five layers of unrelated game logic that have no other reason to know AudioManager exists.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Directory lets the deeply-nested combat code look up AudioManager only when it's actually needed, without forcing five unrelated layers to thread it through as an unused parameter.

quiz.question: What does Service Locator provide?
options: A central registry that code can query to look up shared services by name or type
A guarantee that a class has exactly one instance
A way to clone objects instead of constructing them
A translator between two incompatible interfaces
quiz.answer: A central registry that code can query to look up shared services by name or type
quiz.explanation: Centralized, on-demand lookup — rather than explicit passing — is Service Locator's defining trait.

quiz.question: What's the main downside of Service Locator compared to Dependency Injection?
options: It hides a class's real dependencies inside method bodies instead of making them visible in the constructor
It requires more constructor parameters than DI
It cannot be used in any modern application
quiz.answer: It hides a class's real dependencies inside method bodies instead of making them visible in the constructor
quiz.explanation: This hidden-dependency trade-off is exactly why most modern guidance favors DI where it's practical.

quiz.question: When might Service Locator be a reasonable choice over DI?
options: When a dependency is rarely used deep in a call chain, and threading it through many unrelated layers would be impractical
When you want dependencies to be fully visible in every constructor
When testability is the top priority
When the codebase has no framework or engine conventions around global registries
quiz.answer: When a dependency is rarely used deep in a call chain, and threading it through many unrelated layers would be impractical
quiz.explanation: This narrow, practical trade-off is where Service Locator's convenience can outweigh DI's visibility benefits.

quiz.question: What's a real-world use of Service Locator?
options: Game engines' global manager registries for looking up shared systems like audio or physics
quiz.answer: Game engines' global manager registries for looking up shared systems like audio or physics
quiz.explanation: Game engines are one of the most common real-world contexts where Service Locator-style global lookups are an established convention.
